'''Rolle’s theorem''' states:

If function $f:\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfies

# $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$,
# $f$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$,
# $f(a)=f(b)$,

$$
\exists c\in(a,b), \dot{f}(c)=0.
$$

== Proof in $\mathbb{R}$ ==

If $f=C, C \in \mathbb{R}$:

$$
\forall c \in (a,b), \dot{f}(c)=0,
$$

Else:

Let $L=f(a), f(b)$,

$$
\exists \{c_k\} \in (a,b): f(c) \neq L
$$

Since $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$

$$
\exists c_1 \in \{c_k\}:f(c_1)=f_{\max}[a,b] \lor f_{\min}[a,b]
$$

By [[Fermat's theorem in calculus]], $\dot f(c_1)=0$
